The response to warfarin and dosing re- quirements vary widely between individuals and between differ- ent racial groups.1 Factors involved include age, indication for anticoagulation, diet, and use of interacting drugs, but much of the variability appears to be related to genetic polymorphism. Two genes appear to be particularly important: the gene for the cytochrome P450 isoenzyme CYP2C9, the major enzyme in- volved in warfarin metabolism; and the gene for vitamin K epox- ide reductase (VKOR), which is involved in the synthesis of clot- ting factors and is the major target for warfarin and other coumarin anticoagulants.2 Although polymorphisms in either gene may affect dose requirements, patients with variant alleles for both genes appear to be particularly sensitive to warfarin;3 initial variability in response may be more strongly associated with VKOR.4 Identification of affected patients by genetic test- ing may be used to guide initial warfarin dosage, and a dosage algorithm has been suggested, although it requires validation.5 Similar effects have also been noted with other coumarins, in- cluding acenocoumarol6 and phenprocoumon.7 1.
